posts.c: Have you discovered this North Bennington treasure yet? @parkmccullough is one of the most beautifully preserved Victorian mansions in New England; a grand 1864 estate surrounded by rolling lawns, towering trees, and miles of peaceful walking trails. Even if the mansion is closed for the season, the grounds are open year-round, and they’re stunning in every kind of weather. It’s one of my favorite places to wander with our dogs, soak up a little local history, and bring out-of-state visitors when we want to show off a true Vermont gem. The Mile-Around Woods trail starts right on the property, making it the perfect spot for an adventurous afternoon that blends nature with history. The house reopens for tours on summer weekends and stays open through fall foliage, with special events that make the property feel even more magical. If you’ve been, what’s your favorite part of the estate? If not… add this one to your list. Share this with someone who wants a peaceful walk steeped in hstory,

posts.c: Jason Baumer, a fancy little gent who is apparently too good to enjoy a regular cup of coffee, drank a cup of tea Sunday. The 29-year-old web designer prepared and consumed his precious tea, which is imported from some la-di-da foreign country, at about 10:30 a.m with the loving attention of a brittle, shawl-wearing spinster. “I normally have some Earl Grey in the morning,” said Baumer, referring to a kind of tea named after a guy who used to run around England in a powdered wig and fruity tights. “Sometimes I have toast [and jam] too. Or just a bowl of cereal when I’m in a rush.” Instead of simply heating a mug of water in the microwave, Baumer used a hoity-toity copper-bottomed tea kettle, which His Lordship reportedly purchased at Pier One Imports in 2003 for the express purpose of tea-making. Baumer’s beverage is made with the use of a tea bag, a prissy little package of delicately scented, finely shredded leaves wrapped in a thin gauze and festooned with a bright yellow label tied
posts.cp: Jason Baumer, a fancy little gent who is apparently too good to enjoy a regular cup of coffee, drank a cup of tea Sunday

posts.c: Health insurance premiums for Vermont teachers are poised to see their smallest increase in nearly two decades. The Vermont Education Health Initiative, a self-insured trust that manages health benefits for about 33,000 school employees and their families, announced proposed premium hikes late last month that will average 2.5% next school year. That’s the smallest increase since the 2009-2010 school year. The health trust’s premium increases offer further evidence that Vermont’s laser focus on bringing down prices — particularly at hospitals — is mitigating a healthcare affordability crisis that at one point threatened to bankrupt the state’s largest insurer. Healthcare utilization appears to be cooling somewhat, according to VEHI officials. But the primary driver behind more reasonable premium increases is the underlying cost of care. Read the full story at the link in our bio. Photo by April McCullum/Vermont Public.
posts.cp: Health insurance premiums for Vermont teachers are poised to see their smallest increase in nearly two decades

posts.c: Hi! Jenny, @jenny_teck, here, Senior Social Media Manager at Condé Nast Traveller Germany. I'm just back from Namibia—and I’m still thinking about this trip! Just 50 kilometers south of Windhoek lies Waldeck Lodge (@waldecknamibia), a private retreat surrounded by 16,000 hectares of wilderness. With six beautiful villas and incredible wildlife, it gives you the feeling of having an entire nature reserve to yourself. And that’s exactly how it works: The lodge is booked exclusively for up to 16 guests at a time. Our days started with safaris, spotting giraffes, zebras, antelopes, and hippos—with the possibility of seeing leopards and cheetahs, too. And in between? We spent afternoons by the pool overlooking the hippos, enjoying massages, and soaking in a freestanding tub with views straight into the wilderness. But what really stayed with me was the people. posts.c: For the second year running, an annual tally found a modest decrease in the number of people experiencing homelessness in Vermont. “On its face, this is an encouraging finding. We certainly want to see fewer people experiencing homelessness in Vermont, and any movement in that direction is worth acknowledging,” said Kim Anetsberger, director of the Lamoille Community House and co-chair of the Balance of State Continuum of Care, at a press conference revealing the January count’s results on Tuesday. But the tally, designed to be a yearly snapshot rather than a comprehensive census of everyone experiencing homelessness throughout a given year, gives limited insight, she added. Read the full story at the link in our bio. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger.

posts.c: Between teaching painting, communications work, and the many moving parts of public art, studio has been a hard reach, but I’m always (over and over) finding my way back to my own studio practice. Sometimes the studio itself feels like a habit I have fallen out of; the space is so overwhelming when I return, I don’t know where to start. Recently, though, I’ve found drawing and little making sessions throughout the week make those precious studio sessions so much more vibrant, tactile, and generative. These days, the paintings have strayed from the “work plan,” the “proposal” or “elevator pitch.” That’s all relegated to keeping the public art, communications, and teaching curriculum to their strict but messy timelines. posts.c: Powering up research!☀️⚡ Last week, space station astronauts installed the eighth and final roll-out solar array (ROSA), completing a five-year power upgrade. Roll-out solar arrays have a lightweight and compact design that launches as a cylinder and unfurls like a yoga mat after installation. Despite being about half the size of the legacy arrays, the eight additional roll-out solar arrays boost the station’s power generation by more than 160 kilowatts. Together, the arrays provide increased power for daily operations and hundreds of research investigations that benefit humanity and support future exploration missions. Following prior testing on space station, the roll-out solar arrays have also been used on NASA’s Dart mission, showcasing space station’s essential role as a testbed for the technologies needed for expeditions beyond Earth’s orbit.

posts.c: Croix Bethune has always been a certified athlete—and growing up in a military family played a major role in shaping her soccer career. posts.c: Each Tuesday this season, we're sharing stories that highlight what Rock Point means to you! "Healthy, accessible and welcoming natural areas are key to a thriving city. Calling all teachers, educators and homeschoolers: now is the time to sign up for Scat & Tracks! This fun, educational program is designed to get students from kindergarten through eighth grade outside and exploring Vermont's landscapes and local wildlife by giving educators the plans and support they need to lead nature hikes on school or nearby grounds. Each week for four weeks, students will watch a pre-recorded video that focuses on one Vermont species and covers topics such as habitat, lifecycle and natural history facts. After the video, the students head outside with their teacher to look for the appropriate habitat of the animal that was featured, paying close attention to scat, tracks, and other signs of the critter. This year's featured species includes moose, long-tailed weasel, eastern cottontail, and red fox! The deadline to register is December 15th. Don't wait! Sign up today at https://www.vtfishandwildlife.com/learn-more/conservation-education/scat-and-tracks-program

posts.c: A Statement from the City of Burlington The City of Burlington is committed to building and sustaining respectful, meaningful relationships with the Missisquoi Abenaki and the broader Indigenous communities with historical and contemporary ties to this region. I want to be clear that the City Council’s decision on May 18th not to accept the proposed statue to replace the former Chief Greylock statue was a municipal decision about public art; it was not intended to question or invalidate the identity or heritage of the Missisquoi Abenaki. As a Vermont municipality, the City accepts the State’s recognition of the Missisquoi Abenaki as one of the four indigenous tribes of Vermont, per S.222 (Act 107). We recognize that there are differing perspectives and deeply held concerns regarding identity, history, and representation among communities with connections to this land. posts.c: "We love the kind of travel that winter stirs up in us, be it getting cozy by a fire after a run on the slopes or an unapologetic escape to wherever still has beach weather. In our December issue, we explore both. On the cover, we have Canada's Banff, which has always been a hit for its summertime hiking and lakes but is now leaning fully into the winter season with specialty wellness, activities, and more. We also bring you back to the beaches of Boracay, the perennial favorite island in the Philippines that has undergone a radical transformation over the past decade to ensure it can welcome visitors for years to come. Down in Australia, the city of Brisbane has been quietly reinventing itself, using all its own charm to lure in a global crowd, while back here in New York, Awkwafina takes us on a tour of Manhattan's Koreatown to promote her new Netflix show that spotlights immigrant communities at home. There is also a look at the best Winter Sun getaways from Tahiti to the Caribbean,

posts.c: Across the National Park System, forts, battlefields, historic homes and coastal defenses preserve the places where military history unfolded, and the stories of the people who lived it. At Minute Man National Historical Park, follow the route where the opening battles of the American Revolution began. At Gettysburg National Military Park, walk through the landscape that witnessed one of the Civil War’s defining battles. At Fort McHenry National Monument & Historic Shrine, discover the story behind the flag that inspired “The Star-Spangled Banner.” And at Pearl Harbor National Memorial, remember the lives forever changed by the events of December 7, 1941. From Revolutionary War battlefields to World War II installations and Cold War defenses, these places connect us to generations of service, sacrifice and the lasting impact of conflict. This Veterans Day, step into history, discover the stories behind these places, and honor those who served. Explore America’s military heritage in nat

posts.c: ⏳Get ready to sift through the sands of time when the Architecture + Design Film Series returns to Contois Auditorium on Wednesday, November 11 with a screening of “The Desert of Forbidden Art” at 6:30 pm! Join us for everyone’s favorite movie night that you can catch on the big screen or stream from home via our link in bio. ⁠ ⁠ Prepare to go back in time during Stalin’s Soviet era, where Igor Savitsky collected more than 40,000 avant-garde works of art. These works were considered at odds with the drab realism favored by the government, put the artists at great risk. Savitsky went on to create a museum in Uzbekistan to preserve and protect cultural artifacts from political censorship. Come along for a dramatic journey of sacrifice for the sake of creative freedom, while taking in glorious works of arts and the stories of the people behind them ⁠ ⁠ Swing by Contois Auditorium from 6-6:30pm to mingle with community and neighbors alike while enjoying some complimentary light bites from

posts.c: On display at the Visitor Center this month: bright and evocative Vermont landscape paintings from @laurelwatersart. Stop by and admire these swirling, colorful original paintings and prints. Laurel is a local artist inspired by nature. She began her adult life in Vermont working in the Green Mountains as a wilderness therapy guide. On her shifts "out of field", she maintained an art studio, where she could connect the influence of nature with her own creativity and artistic intuition. Laurel describes a "Rich symbiosis [that] unfolded between the protected Vermont nature, and the protection for her own "safely wild" creative voice, like Nature was holding up a mirror for her inner possibility palette as well." She sells paper and canvas prints, and takes original commissions. "Vancouver’s most VIBRANT neighborhood is historic Chinatown," says CNT Local Creator @ben.glassco. "It's the largest in Canada and stands as a living, breathing heartbeat of the city…and Canada itself. The Gold Rush of the 1850s first brought Chinese migrants to the West Coast, and soon thousands of laborers infamously gave their lives on the Canadian Pacific Railway. Few communities accepted Chinese migrants, so they were forced to build their own. Chinatown rose above systemic persecution to become the center of trade, nightlife, and culture in the new 'Western Canada.' Today, steaming woks, trendy pop-ups, and vibrant speakeasies still fill the gritty but exciting streets—a testament to 150 years of tenacity from the founding peoples of our country." — CNT Local Creator @ben.glassco @ben.glassco's Top Recommendations: Newtown Bakery (slide 7) @chinatownbbq @thechineseteashop by Daniel Lui (slide 12) @chinatownstorytellingcentre (slide 15) @whereisbagheera (slide 4) @baldyloxvintage

posts.c: Have you ever wondered how a forest changes over its lifetime? Biodiverse forest communities depend on interconnected forest habitats that vary in age and forest structure. Early successional, or young forests, like the one illustrated here feature canopy gaps that allow sunlight to reach the forest floor. These gaps are created by forest disturbances, including natural events like windstorms as well as carefully planned forest management. Removing a few trees creates space and opportunity for a new generation of trees and diverse communities of plants, fungi, and wildlife. These changes can happen all at once or gradually over time and can affect just a small area or several acres. Get started fostering biodiversity in your forest. Check out the @uvmextforestry's new Forest Biodiversity website for educational guides and stewardship resources. Developed in partnership with @audubonvermont, @vtcoverts, Vermont Biodiversity Alliance, @vtforestsparksrecreation, and @vwatreefarm . 🔗Link i

posts.c: Earth’s protective ozone layer is still on track for long-term recovery, despite a larger Antarctic ozone hole this year. The 2026 ozone hole is the 7th-largest ozone hole since NASA began tracking it in 1979. This year, the ozone hole reached its maximum extent of 10.5 million square miles on September 18. However, the ozone hole could have been 1 to 2 million square miles larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were two decades ago. posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👀 Woodstock was originally expected to attract around 50,000 people, but approximately 400,000 showed up. Held in August 1969 on a dairy farm in Bethel, New York, the legendary music festival became so overcrowded that organizers abandoned ticket collection and effectively made it free. Despite massive traffic jams, food shortages, rain, and muddy conditions, Woodstock became a defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture. Interestingly, some of the biggest musicians of the era never performed at Woodstock, including The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and Led Zeppelin. Jimi Hendrix famously closed the festival on Monday morning, playing to a much smaller crowd after most attendees had already left. Despite its reputation as a chaotic disaster, Woodstock became one of the most celebrated music events in history. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: This is how photography changes the world 🌎 This is the first-ever time that the mating ritual of Abbott’s moray eels has ever been seen. Tony Wu (@tonywu98) has studied this male since 2024 to be able to get this landmark picture to help biologists understand the courtship of these animals. Guided only by a dim red-light source, and using a customised fisheye camera lens, Tony was able to capture the eel visiting females that dwell in crevices all across the reef while minimising the amount of disturbance. The observations from Tony’s work are now feeding into published scientific studies. 📸 ‘Making Morays’ is the winner of the Underwater category of this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year. Book your tickets for #WPY62 now via the link in our bio! #WPY #WildlifePhotographerOfTheYear #WildlifePhotography #NaturePhotography #NaturalHistoryMuseum #MorayEel
posts.cp: This is how photography changes the world

posts.c: This Native American Heritage Month, we honor Allard, a historian, Water Protector, and Dakota matriarch whose leadership spark the Standing Rock movement. As the founder of Sacred Stone Camp, she brought together Indigenous communities and allies to protect water, land, sacred sites, and Tribal sovereignty in the face of the Dakota Access Pipeline. Before becoming internationally known as an activist, Allard spent decades preserving the history, culture, and sacred sites of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. She believed that protecting ancestral lands and cultural heritage was a responsibility owed to future generations, often reminding others that Indigenous history is not a story of the distant past, but a living history that continues today. Throughout her life, Allard advocated for the protection of what she called "our first medicine," water. Her legacy continues to inspire movements for environmental justice, Indigenous rights, and cultural preservation across the world. As we cele

posts.c: 👯 Identical twins develop from a single fertilised egg that splits into two embryos, which means they share virtually the same DNA. This is why they can look almost indistinguishable from each other, with matching facial features, build, and even mannerisms. Studies have found that identical twins often think alike, make similar choices, and react to situations in the same way, even when raised apart, suggesting that genetics plays a surprisingly large role in shaping personality and behaviour alongside environment. (🎥/ @twintakeover80 )

posts.c: 🍒 Bananas are berries, but strawberries aren’t technically berries. Botanically, bananas qualify as berries because they develop from a single flower’s ovary, while strawberries are classified as aggregate accessory fruits. Even more surprisingly, pineapples aren’t single fruits either. They’re formed when dozens of individual flowers fuse together into one large fruit. Interestingly, apples float because roughly 25% of their volume is air, while watermelons are about 92% water. Some fruits can also continue ripening after being picked, including bananas and avocados, while others, like strawberries, do not ripen significantly once harvested. And despite their name, oranges aren’t always orange. In tropical climates, ripe oranges can remain green because warm temperatures prevent their green chlorophyll from fully breaking down. posts.c: This week's #WPY62 guest is our Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Federico Veronesi (@federico_veronesi)! 🤩 This week, Federico will share seven more powerful stories from the African continent with us. Today, he explores a scene that moved him similarly to his award-winning image in our competition. "Before capturing my recent overall winning image 'The Aftermath' in September 2025 in Namibia, I had come across another very moving scene involving the elephants’ relationship with death. Wrapped by the hazy blue light filtering through the trees, so typical of this area, there was an elephant family standing guard around the half-decomposed carcass of another elephant. posts.c: We have Chrysanthemum Festival down to a science. 👉 Swipe to find out how our growers perfected their techniques to create a display that builds on centuries of history and decades of innovation. Some of our chrysanthemum forms require a little tough horticultural love! During training, our gardeners allow the plants to wilt slightly, making their stems more pliable so they can be carefully shaped around custom metal frameworks. (There are very few plants that are willing to grow and bloom in a spiral!) Mums are short-day plants, meaning they naturally begin to develop flower buds as the nights grow longer in the fall. But at Longwood, we use a little horticultural know-how to time their blooms just right for Chrysanthemum Festival. By carefully controlling their exposure to light and darkness, our growers can encourage the plants to bloom right on schedule. Many of our mum forms are grafted onto Artemisia rootstock to benefit from its strong root system and resistance to summer heat,

@royalgorgerouterr is a 150-year-old route winding along the Arkansas River, a geological wonder nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of the Arkansas River.” Visitors can experience the dramatic 10-mile-long chasm from several perspectives: From above, while gazing down from the Royal Gorge Bridge, the tallest suspension bridge in the nation (or for more adventurous travelers, while rock climbing a 5-hour via ferrata); and from below, while paddling the Arkansas’s roaring rapids on a whitewater raft. But for travelers looking to sit back and savor the scenery passing by, there's no better viewpoint than the Royal Gorge Route Railroad's open-air car, standing face-to-face with the staggering canyon walls. Read @kutasarah's full story of her front-row seat to one of Colorado’s greatest natural wonders at the link in bio.

posts.c: Cats can recognize their owner’s voice but sometimes deliberately choose not to respond. Research shows that domestic cats can distinguish familiar human voices from strangers, yet they often react with little more than an ear twitch or head movement. Interestingly, cats also have an extraordinary righting reflex that helps them twist their bodies midair and land on their feet, although falls can still seriously injure them. Another surprising fact is that cats have roughly 200 million odor-sensitive receptors in their noses, giving them a remarkably powerful sense of smell. Their whiskers help them detect nearby objects and navigate tight spaces, while their flexible spines allow impressive jumps. Cats also spend around 12 to 16 hours sleeping daily, meaning they have somehow perfected a lifestyle built around eating, napping, and occasionally acknowledging their owners. Like this content? posts.c: On National Bison Day, we celebrate one of America’s most iconic animals and a powerful symbol of strength and resilience. Once reduced to fewer than 1,000 individuals, bison have made a remarkable comeback thanks to decades of dedicated conservation efforts. Today, the National Park Service supports 19 bison herds across 12 states, helping ensure these magnificent animals continue to roam the landscape. Of course, majestic doesn’t mean approachable. Bison are wild, unpredictable, and considerably less interested in meeting you than you might be in meeting them. No matter how calm or cow-like they appear, always stay at least 25 yards away. Finally, if you encounter bison on the road, remember: they’re in no hurry, and your schedule is not their concern. Slow down, stay in your vehicle, and patiently wait for them to move along. Honking or driving aggressively toward bison won’t make them move faster. In fact, it may have the opposite effect. NPS photos

posts.c: One of the things I find most extraordinary about polar bears is the immense journeys they undertake over a lifetime. Guided by a sense of smell seven times more powerful than a blood hound’s, they can detect a seal hidden beneath layers of snow and ice from more than half a mile away. They spend much of their lives following invisible trails of scent across hundreds of miles of Arctic wilderness. This is also how they find one another across a vast, seemingly desolate landscape, although finding mates has become more of a challenge as sea ice recedes. They are the great nomads of the Arctic, always inquisitive, resourceful, and, above all, fiercely determined to navigate a formidable and ever-changing world. For those interested in owning one of my polar bear prints, please visit the link in my bio or visit my website to submit an inquiry. From now until Christmas, all fine art purchases come with a copy of my new book Reverence.

posts.c: It's #NationalBisonDay, and we've got some bison facts! 1️⃣ Bison are the largest land mammal in North America Male bison (bulls) weigh up to 2,000 pounds and stand 6 feet tall, while females (cows) weigh up to 1,000 pounds and reach a height of 4-5 feet. Bison calves can weigh 30–70 pounds at birth. 2️⃣ Bison may be big, but they're also fast They are extremely agile and can run up to 30 miles per hour! 3️⃣ You can judge a bison's mood by its tail When it hangs down and swishes naturally, the bison is usually calm. If the tail is standing straight up, watch out! It may be ready to charge. No matter what a bison's tail is doing though, remember that they are unpredictable and can charge at any moment. Every year, there are regrettable accidents caused by people getting too close to these massive animals. It's great to love the bison but always be sure to love them from a distance of at least 25 yards (23 meters). 4️⃣ Bison love a good salad They primarily eat grasses, weeds and leafy p

posts.c: Climb ev’ry mountain, Gnaw ev’ry tree, The summit is calling, Living the porcupine dream. Porcupines are creatures of habit. They can spend days hanging out in the same tree, nibbling on bark and needles and quite content with their accommodations. But this particular porcupine has other plans. Not content to keep its paws at lower elevations, it’s steadily making its way uphill, navigating rocks and small plants with the determination of someone who has decided the grass really is greener higher up. Perhaps there’s a better tree waiting at the top. Perhaps it’s simply looking for a change of scenery. What we do know is that this porcupine is going places….mostly uphill. Perhaps to find its dream. NPS video/R. Buchanan: A porcupine walks uphill amid rocks and small plants @mountrainiernps Music of Climb every mountain plays.

posts.c: Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar invites the young and young at heart to connect with ocean life through movement and play. The ocean moves us! Hold on like a seahorse—there are plenty of them here and so much more to discover! Just swipe left and sea. African penguins are back in a newly expanded habitat! Watch as they groom and dive off the rocks. Then, practice your penguin waddle in this new interactive space. A 20-foot-long coral reef includes giant clams and a bluespotted ribbontail ray that glides along the sand. Nearby, clownfish nestle into anemones. Enjoy multiple play areas that are welcoming to visitors of all ages. There’s also plenty of rest areas to relax and check out the ocean views of Monterey Bay! Watch leaping blennies hop across wet stones! Visitors can also follow shapes in the floor to hop from rock to rock like blennies. There’s so much to discover in Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar from flamboyant cuttlefish to garden eels. Swim over to the link in bio for

posts.c: Fall is calling. The leaves are changing, the air is getting crisp, and suddenly everyone thinks they’re an experienced outdoorsperson because they put on a flannel shirt. Before you head out to admire the fall foliage, it’s important to do a little homework. Ugh, homework? It’s not that bad. And will maybe save you on the paperwork later. In fact, a little planning can go a long way toward making your autumn adventure enjoyable (and keeping it from becoming an unexpected survival exercise). 🍂 Know before you go: Check the park’s website for current conditions, trail closures, weather forecasts, and seasonal changes. Fall weather can be unpredictable, just like your uncle’s stories at Thanksgiving. 🥾 Choose your adventure wisely: Pick trails and activities that match your experience and abilities. Not every scenic overlook requires a 12-mile hike and questionable life choices. 🎒 Pack the essentials: Bring water, food, appropriate layers, and a map. Your phone is useful, but it isn’t a

posts.c: If you want to try a ribbon chain garland for the holidays, one of the best parts is how easy they are to store! ✨🌈 I literally throw them in the top of a storage bin. Make sure they’re loose and not smashed. They come out wrinkle free and ready to go for another year! Paper will not store this nicely! For these, I used 1.5” wide grosgrain ribbon. Each piece is cut to 8”. This will be my third year using these and they’re still in perfect shape 🙌🏻 Would you try these in your home? They’re so fun for the room the Christmas tree is in! 🎄

posts.c: What was at stake when Whitney Houston, after spending the decade as a movie star, returned to the R&B charts in 1998? This week on the NPR+ series ‘Over and Over,’ Ann Powers and Daoud Tyler-Ameen discuss “It’s Not Right but It’s Okay,” the comeback smash that dared to return the tabloids’ gaze.⁠ ⁠ Topics include Houston’s “homegirl diva” era, the genre-realigning sound of producer Rodney “Darkchild” Jerkins, and how an adultery lament morphed into a queer club anthem. Plus, some expert insights from scholar Emily Lordi (@emilylordi1), author of ‘Holding Lightning: The Life, Loves, and Art of Whitney Houston.’⁠ ⁠ Find the full episode, and sign up for NPR+, at the link in our bio.

Home Ice Advantage, Higher Ground, and Striations of Time. As the holidays approach, my thoughts keep returning to Antarctica and how the continent must be stirring to life. With the polar summer fast approaching, Adélie and chinstrap penguins are building their nests and laying eggs. Icebergs sculpted by millennia of densely-packed snowfall glow blue beneath the returning light and provide young penguins refuge from leopard seals. It is one of the most spectacular sights in the world, though I also cannot help thinking of how long it will last between a changing climate and commercial fisheries exploiting its waters. My hope in sharing images like the ones above is that we recognize the beauty of what is at stake and take action to protect it. To inquire about prints and explore more of my work across the poles, visit the link in my bio. From now until Christmas, all fine art purchases come with a copy of my book Reverence.

posts.c: Hubble (along with ground-based telescopes) revealed that the expansion rate of our universe is accelerating! Soon, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will study the “dark energy” behind this expansion with its large field of view and infrared vision. Its treasure trove of data will include tens of thousands of exploding stars and hundreds of millions of distant galaxies, tracing the universe’s expansion across nearly all of cosmic history! Hubble's key observations led to dark energy's discovery (even helping earn a Nobel prize in physics!) and the mission will work with Roman to continue investigating this enigma. As we gear up for its first images, we'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy. Check the link in our bio for more! #NASA #Hubble #Roman #astrophysics #space

You've likely heard of geysers and hot springs, but what about fumaroles? Fumaroles (or steam vents) are the hottest hydrothermal features in Yellowstone, with temperatures up to 280 F (138 C)! 🔥 Because they are so hot and contain very little water, the water boils away before reaching the surface. Then, steam and other gases emerge from the feature's vent, sometimes making hissing or whistling sounds. Roaring Mountain is a wonderful place to enjoy the sights and sounds of fumaroles, especially on cooler days! 👉 Learn more about fumaroles at: go.nps.gov/YELLhydrothermalfeatures (link in our "Learn More" highlight) Photo (NPS / Ashton Hooker): Roaring Mountain on a chilly winter day.

posts.c: Did you know that the sprawling beauty of Chrysanthemum Festival all starts … 🧪… in a test tube?! As stewards of one of North America’s largest and oldest collections of chrysanthemums, we rely on exacting science to ensure this beauty endures. posts.c: When choosing the images for my book Reverence, I let go of the photojournalist mindset honed over decades of working as a National Geographic photographer and looked instead for the images that sparked some kind of emotion within. The Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas) are truly a place of extremes, battered by powerful, nutrient-dense currents that pummel the cliffs and feed the towering kelp forests below the surface. The density of life here is staggering, especially on Steeple Jason where conservationists had the foresight to reclaim the island from sheep farming as far back as the 70s. Today the island is under the guardianship of the Wildlife Conservation Society and its natural legacy is preserved as one of the last wild places on Earth.

posts.c: Each autumn, we return to Twilight of the Idols, our seasonal porter brewed with coffee and cinnamon and conditioned on vanilla beans. Its origins precede Hill Farmstead, reaching back to Denmark in 2009. Shaun and Ryan Witter-Merithew first met in 2007. Two years later, as Shaun prepared to leave his brewing position at Nørrebro Bryghus and Fanø Bryghus, he enticed Ryan to move to Denmark to assume the role. They lived and brewed together for a month, beginning a friendship and collaboration that continues today. During that overlap, they established Grassroots Brewing to continue making beer together and maintain their connection to Denmark. Working on their first Christmas beer together (Fanø’s JulePorter), the idea for what would become Twilight of the Idols emerged from this period, taking its name from Friedrich Nietzsche’s text. posts.c: My BBC story on Quebecois profanity has its very own content warning — and some extremely NSFW French-language cursing. (Which I've been obsessed with since I was a baby linguist at Berkeley.) Quebec is "the Amazon rainforest of swear words," according to one expert, a reference to a lexicon so large, varied and colorful it outstrips most of the planet's 7,000-odd languages. I'm grateful to editor extraordinaire @eliot.stein for letting me write about my favorite foul-mouthed neighbors to the north, whose vocabulary is far better suited to recent political shenanigans than anything English can produce. ("Ostie consacrée au cul de cochon" is now my official position on this "51st state" business.) Thanks to the linguistics, historians, and experts — including @frenchwithfrederic and Michelle Bélanger of @museepop in Trois-Rivières — who spoke with me for the piece. And many thanks to the patrons of the wonderful Bar Sainte-Angèle for providing a few juicy exemplars during a recent visit

What if your fence could grow food instead of just taking up space? A fruit fence turns a simple vertical structure into a productive growing system, and passion fruit is perfect for the job because its climbing tendrils naturally grip onto nearby supports. The science is pretty cool. Passion fruit vines grow rapidly, spreading their leaves across a trellis to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. With enough light, water, and nutrients, the plant converts that energy into vigorous growth and eventually flowers and fruit. Training the vines vertically also helps you use space more efficiently, turning an otherwise unused area into productive growing space. And here’s the best part: a well-established passion fruit vine can produce an impressive harvest while giving you a living privacy screen. Instead of building a fence that only blocks the view, why not grow one that hides the eyesores, adds greenery, and produces delicious fruit? That’s a whole lot more value from the same footprint.

posts.c: Hello again, M30! This new image shows a globular star cluster, which is a roughly spherical grouping of stars held together by gravity. Because of Hubble's long life, it's been able to observe M30 multiple times and track how different populations of stars in globular clusters move. Hubble can discern incredibly specific details in distant objects, allowing for this unprecedented "long-form" astronomy. Discover more at the link in our bio! Image description: A star cluster seen up close, filling the view with thousands of stars. They are clearly divided between blue ones, which are scattered around the outskirts of the image but more towards the center and are the majority in the bright core of the cluster, and yellow stars, which are present in the core but make up most of the cluster outside of that. A few orange stars are closer to us and appear noticeably larger. Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini #NASA #Hubble #news #stars #space
posts.hd: Hubble image of globular star cluster M30

posts.c: A season of low rain can turn an island into a beach… come explore! ☀️ The Colchester Causeway is a famous rec path that carves through Lake Champlain. It’s usually surrounded on all sides by water, but not this year. A dry summer and fall have left a “beach” between the rail trail and Law Island. ⭐️ Law Island is located about half a mile from where the Causeway meets the bay. Most of the bay has some water right now, but the area around the island is dry. You can walk or bike right to it! Last year, Vermont had a historic drought that dropped the lake by 8 feet. This was the first time in 72 years that the lake lost this much water. I posted two videos that went viral of the “islands” at Kill Kare State Park and Colchester Causeway. We were all in shock that we could walk to these islands! 🐠 Now, a year later, it feels surreal to walk to Law Island again. I didn’t feel the same sense of “adventure” as last year… maybe because the media told us this would be a “once in a lifetime” thi

posts.c: Small plants need love too! So I try to find a fun way to style them instead of just placing them in a standard terra cotta pot. Here, I took this 4” birkin philodendron and cut the perfect piece of cork to surround its roots. Instead of glue a stainless steel mesh base to the cork, like I typically do, I used a low planter to work as the base of the “pot” to hold in the soil. Obviously it has drainage holes for those that were about to ask 😉 I then dressed up the topsoil with live moss and called it a day. It might be small but it makes a strong statement 💚🌿 #plants #plantstyling #design #beforeandafter #babygirl Low planter from @fayraystudio

posts.c: Have you ever wondered how birds stay warm during winter? Chickadees grow feathers that can keep them up to 100 degrees F warmer than the surrounding air temperature. Waterfowl exhibit counter-current heat exchange in their limbs, which enables them to stand in cold water. Other adaptations include roosting with heads tucked into back feathers to conserve heat and staying active by retrieving food stored during the autumn months. 👉 Want to learn more? posts.c: Each fall, landlocked Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) leave the open waters of Lake Champlain and make their way upstream, navigating currents and rocky riverbeds to reach their spawning grounds. Often referred to as a salmon run, this seasonal journey takes place in rivers throughout the Lake Champlain watershed, including the Ausable, Boquet, and Winooski rivers. Beginning in early September and continuing through mid-November, this remarkable event is made challenging by barriers to movement and habitat degradation. The future of landlocked Atlantic salmon depends on our ability to restore and protect the river corridors essential to their survival. Read our full Lake Look column - An Upriver Journey - through the link in our bio🔗

posts.c: The ultimate group project: studying worlds beyond our own. As we get closer to the first images from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a long list of science objectives await. One way Roman will team up with Hubble is by the different ways the missions will study exoplanets. An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than our Sun. Roman will likely find hundreds of thousands exoplanets with its remarkable instruments; meanwhile, Hubble’s capabilities allow for analysis of exoplanet atmospheres. This work is part of NASA's search for life elsewhere in the universe. Plus, Roman's coronograph instrument will be able to directly image some larger exoplanets. We'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy in the weeks to come. Check the link in our bio for more on Hubble and Roman! posts.c: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one. 🎨 A recent University College London study found that more frequent engagement in arts and cultural activities was associated with slower biological aging. Weekly arts participants showed a 4% slower pace of aging than those who rarely participated. Here’s why this matters for play. Art is one way we play. When we paint, dance, make music, experiment with materials, or create something alongside others, we’re engaging in the very things that make play powerful: curiosity, imagination, expression, and exploration. The research gives us another reason to take these experiences seriously. Play isn’t just entertainment or a break from real life. It’s part of how we nurture our creativity, connection, and vitality. Make something. Move something. Try something new. Give yourself the gift ofplay. #PlayIntention #PowerOfPlay #CreativeWellbeing #ArtsAndHealt
posts.cp: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one

posts.c: One of the densest concentrations of geysers in Yellowstone can be found in the remote Shoshone Geyser Basin, on the west side of Shoshone Lake. We visit the area in the latest Yellowstone Volcano Observatory monthly video update. 🌊 Shoshone Geyser Basin is one of the most spectacular in all of Yellowstone National Park. Located deep in the backcountry along the west side of Shoshone Lake, the area has one of the densest concentrations of geysers, second only to the Upper Geyser Basin (where Old Faithful is located). There are over 100 geysers in this region and 40 or 50 might be active at any given time. A trail takes you right by Minute Man geyser (always at the ready!), so it is quite easy to watch the frequent eruptions there. ⚡During the month of October 2026, the University of Utah Seismograph Stations, which monitors and operates the Yellowstone seismic network, located 66 earthquakes. posts.c: A little throwback to my broke college girl dinner era…. Honestly, I forgot how good these things are. Basically everything you want in a pizza, minus having to make an actual pizza. And yes, they’re still just as good as they were at 1AM in college. Here’s how I made them: - Split English muffins in half, drizzle with EVOO, sprinkle with garlic powder, and bake at 400°F for about 10–12 minutes, until lightly golden. - Add marinara, mozzarella, provolone, (or whatever your favorite cheese is!), dried oregano, and a little garlic salt. - Back into the oven until the cheese is melted and bubbly. - Serve with extra warm marinara for dipping. Please tell me I’m not the only one who lived on these back in the day….

posts.c: Where's the oxygen? After researchers studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies, they realized much of the oxygen they expected to see was missing. Oxygen is the main element formed by stars, and also the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium. But by using Hubble, these scientists learned that dwarf galaxies can only hang on to a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars. Energy from the low-mass galaxies’ massive stars, along with galactic winds unleashed by supernova explosions, are apparently more effective at driving out the oxygen than current models predict. Read more at the link in our bio! posts.c: Between fall foliage and snow comes Vermont’s most sung-about season: STICK SEASON! 🍂 (Hi, @noahkahanmusic 👋) Here’s what these Vermont experts LOVE about November… 👉 @vermontforreal says to explore historic sites! Stick season is the best time to find pieces of history (otherwise hidden by snow or lush greens). Visit state parks, museums, and nature preserves! posts.c: The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

posts.c: When Halloween is over, look for Dracula in a hibernaculum! A hibernaculum is a place like a cave, den, or burrow, where animals seek shelter for the winter. More surprising is that researchers have documented bat activity in Northern Yellowstone throughout the winter, despite little insect activity, and freezing cold temperatures. #BatWeek

posts.c: Our Orange County tour continues to the Cilley Bridge today. Here is another of the area's many multiple kingpost bridges. The bridge was built in 1883 and rehabilitated in 2006. The Covered Spans of Yesteryear website provides some historical background: "The bridge was named for the nearby Cilley family and was built at a cost of $523.35. When built, its portals were skewed by seven degrees; thus, it exhibits a slight camber. The truss is unusual in that the truss has an upper chord with the vertical tension members extending slightly above the chord to support the roof sill and the roof". #vtcbsinayear #cilleycbvt #tunbridgevt #vermontscoveredbridges #vermontcoveredbridgesociety #coveredspansofyesteryear https://www.vermontbridges.org/orange_county_combined-wcg-phase1_cilley.shtml

posts.c: New Tools for Healthier Soils! We’ve got new equipment at the Intervale Center! Thanks to funding from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board and the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, our new 6-foot seed drill and flail mower will make it easier to plant and manage crops across the Intervale. Right now, we are planting cover crops. Cover crops are planted to protect the soil between growing seasons, rather than for harvest. Their roots hold soil in place, build organic matter, and reduce nutrient runoff; creating a strong, resilient foundation for our food system. The seed drill plants seeds with minimal soil disturbance, and the mower chops down vegetation for quick and efficient turnover back to crop production. Their compact size makes them ideal for smaller farm fields and garden plots in the Intervale that were formerly cover cropped by hand or not at all. posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. posts.c: What is making this sea of sand march inland? ⌛ This timelapse shows the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil, known for its large sand dunes and seasonal rainwater lagoons. Strong winds from the Atlantic Ocean keep these dunes in constant motion. Over the years, the wind steadily pushes the sand, causing the dunes to migrate inland and change the shape of the landscape. Satellite data helps scientists track how remote landscapes change over time. Captured by the joint @nasa and @usgs Landsat program, these natural-color images show over four decades of this moving environment. Video description: A natural-color Landsat time series of Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses National Park spanning from 1984 to 2026. As the video plays, large white sand dunes move steadily inland across the coast. Among the shifting white sand are darker patches of seasonal rainwater lagoons and vegetation. #nasa #earth #science
posts.hd: Timelapse of dunes migrating in Brazil park

posts.c: We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

posts.c: Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. While El Niño occurs in the Pacific Ocean, with changes most visible along the equator, its effects can be felt all around the world. NASA satellites like PACE and Sentinel-6 are equipped to measure some of the key features of the phenomenon. Video description: Three data visualizations stacked vertically show sea surface height, sea surface temperature, and ocean color from January 2026 to September 2026. As it plays, text forms across the screen that reads “We’re experiencing a record El Niño” and transitions to “Swipe to compare the growing 2026 El Niño with a weak La Niña in 2025.” Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

posts.c: You don’t need a garden bed to grow potatoes, and the science behind it is pretty cool. A seed potato already contains the energy and nutrients needed to kickstart new growth. Once it sprouts, the roots pull water and nutrients from the soil, while the leaves capture sunlight and convert it into energy that fuels the development of new potatoes underground. The tricky part is creating the right environment for those tubers. We’re using @foxfarmsoilandfertilizer Ocean Forest soil to give each potato a consistent growing medium with nutrients to support early growth. Potatoes need consistent moisture, but soil that stays too wet can limit oxygen around the roots and encourage rot. Good drainage helps maintain that balance, which is why the container you choose can make a bigger difference than you might expect. That’s what makes this potato experiment so interesting. Different containers can change how quickly soil dries out, how much heat it holds, and how easily excess water escapes. B

posts.c: This planet is haunted! 👻 The ghosts of volcanic eruptions, asteroid strikes, and evaporated lakes here on Earth are visible in echoes seen from space. Explore some of the places on our planet still haunted by the past. A volcanic eruption about 4,000 years ago created the eerily named Deception Island. The horseshoe-shaped island is actually the exposed part of a volcano itself, while the harbor in its center is a phantom of that massive volcanic eruption. As the volcano’s magma chamber emptied, the sudden drop in pressure inside the volcano caused the top to collapse and form a caldera — now called Port Foster. Image description: Landsat 8 image of Deception Island. It is horseshoe shaped and mostly rocky brown. The thin arch of rock comes to a ridge that runs the length of the island, along its center, like a backbone. posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Producer: Paul Morris Special thanks to Candy Jar, ASMR, and Donut Dan Music Credit: "Pizz with Pizzazz" by Bertrand Allagnat [SACEM] via Illustration Musicale [SACEM], Universal Productio

Optical illusions happen because your eyes send information to your brain, and your brain immediately starts making educated guesses about what it is seeing. Usually that works perfectly, but certain patterns, colors, shadows, and shapes can trick those shortcuts, making still images appear to move or identical lines look completely different. The best part is that even after someone explains the illusion, your brain may still refuse to cooperate. You can literally know two squares are the same color and your brain will look you dead in the eye and say, “No, they absolutely are not.” Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

Formulated with Dr. Angela Rollins, a board-certified veterinary nutritionist and clinical professor at the University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine (@utcvm), Vitality intends to reduce inflammation and support overall wellness, especially for picky eaters who aren’t eager for fruits and veggies, like Friedman’s own dog, Elsa. 🐶 The chew enters a market filled with pet multivitamins, which aren’t always a necessary addition to a dog’s diet. held.c: 2 weeks since Kiki’s accident / hip dysplasia diagnosis ❤️ And 2 weeks without walkies for Kiki 🥺 we might do our first short 5 minute walk today, for a change of scenery. Kiki is definitely making sure we’re aware of the fact that she is EXTREMELY BORED. But the more bed rest she gets, the faster we hope she’ll go back to normal! She is now walking normally without limping, but is still lifting her paw when she’s standing still. Very very eager to jump around, but we do find that she’s taking more time to go up the stairs (when we catch her doing it)… instead of zooming upstairs like a breeze, she goes step by step… 🥹 Which is also making us realise that even though they’re still puppies on the inside, they’re getting older on the outside. In fact, it’s Kiki’s 7th birthday in two days! She also has her first hydrotherapy appointment tomorrow ❤️ #dog #beagle

held.c: Last week was tough for us. We were about to go on our daily walk, Kiki was on the couch while I put her harness on, I quickly went upstairs, and when I came back down, she was laying on the floor acting strange. When she got up, she was panting, drooling, and lifting her paw. It was 4pm on a Sunday, which meant the vets were closed. We had to drive 25 minutes to an emergency vet, they gave her pain meds and told us to keep an eye on her. On Monday morning, she was visibly in pain - as you can see in the first few clips. So we took her to the vet again. They told us - she has no noticeable fractures so you can either wait it out with her pain meds, or do an xray to find out more. We wanted to know more. And thank goodness we did… as it turned out, Kiki had hip dysplasia. One that you can tell it has most likely been there since she was a puppy - some dogs get it genetically. The vast majority of us still do things because It helps to lift up our people, not because It is going to make us a billion dollars. This Election Day I will vote for the hard working Americans who deserve a better and easier path forward, and I will vote against the greedy and power obsessed billionaires who think they can run this country. held.c: Rest easy, Captain. We have the helm. ✨ Here is Webb’s look at Westerlund 1, a super star cluster - one of the closest clusters of its kind. Super star clusters are young and contain more than 10,000 times the mass of the Sun packed into a small volume. Westerlund 1 is the most massive yet identified in our galaxy, with 50,000 to 100,000 times the mass of the Sun contained within a region less than six light-years across. Super star clusters are one of the most extreme environments in which stars and planets can form. Because our galaxy is past its peak of star formation, and because such stars live relatively short lives, only a few of these clusters still exist to give us clues to that past era. It’s Pop-up week 🔍 What exactly is “slow looking”? Slow looking is an approach to viewing art that emphasizes our own observations and reflections, rather than familiarity with the artwork or art terminology. It’s also a visual thinking strategy used by first-year medical students in Dr. Sakshi Jasra’s Professionalism, Communication, and Reflection class at the Larner College of Medicine. Now in it’s third year running with the Fleming, we partnered with Dr. Jasra to transform her popular assignment into a pop-up exhibit for all! Now through Saturday, visit the Learning Studio to visit “Double Take” any time during our regular hours and try slow looking for yourself. Featuring a wide range of works from our collections, including a clay tablet from Mesopotamia, a photograph by Carrie Mae Weems, and much more, simply choose a work and follow our prompts. The only thing you need to bring is your own curiosity.

What if you could turn a chicken into part of the process of growing a giant pumpkin? When Gucci, one of my original hens, passed away, I buried her beneath an Atlantic Giant pumpkin. Here’s the cool part: as bacteria and fungi break down organic matter, they recycle nutrients back into the soil. Plants can’t use all those nutrients immediately, though. Decomposition transforms them into forms roots can absorb, making decomposers an incredibly important part of a healthy garden. But growing a giant pumpkin takes more than nutrient-rich soil. I buried the vines so more nodes could develop roots, giving the plant additional access to water and nutrients. I removed competing flowers and fruits to focus the plant’s resources on one pumpkin, then added sand and plywood underneath to support its growing weight. Even with all those tricks, powdery mildew showed up and eventually slowed its growth. That’s what makes giant vegetables so fascinating: genetics, photosynthesis, growing conditions,

In loving memory of my bestest friend and the light of my life, Jax. Rescued by PETA in 2010 at a year old, he was my shadow for the next 16+ years, sharing adventures and cuddles. His big brown eyes could stare into my soul and his big ears heard everything. He had quite the personality and loved to “talk,” and I quickly learned to understand his squeaks and groans. Jax was an excellent travel companion, happy to just be wherever I was. He was a master sunbather, always searching for the coziest spot in the house to catch some rays. In his younger years he loved to hike (and later enjoyed riding along in a backpack), and he was always ready to chase tennis balls or play tug-o’ -war until we were both exhausted. Then, he’d cuddle up next to me under a blanket, burrow his nose in, and snore and dream. At the end, with his face and muzzle nearly white, he was declining quickly and ready to go, and I was grateful to be able to give him a peaceful goodbye. Life isn’t the same without him,
held.cp: In loving memory of my bestest friend and the light of my life, Jax
